item.content:encoded:
The Braves powered their way to an NLDS berth after taking out their division rivals.
On Thursday night, Atlanta won a winner-take-all Game 3 against the Phillies, 6–2, in front of a loud Truist Park crowd. The Braves tagged Philadelphia starter Aaron Nola for three runs in the bottom of the first inning and never looked back, leading wire-to-wire to eliminate their NL East peers.
Surprise starter Ray Kerr, a 32-year-old with 72 2/3 career MLB innings, pitched into the fourth inning unscathed to keep the Phillies at arm’s length. The Phillies never found much offense beyond contributions from stars Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber, as the supporting cast beyond Alec Bohm failed to step up.
The victory sends Atlanta to Los Angeles for an NLDS matchup with the Dodgers starting on Saturday. For Philadelphia, a season that began with World Series ambitions was cut short in the wild-card round.
Here are our three takeaways from Game 3.
Braves Slug Their Way to NLDS
Atlanta relied heavily on the long ball in 2026, and with its season on the line that’s what it used to punch a ticket to the NLDS.
The Braves’ 204 regular season home runs ranked seventh in baseball, while their collective .409 slugging percentage was sixth. In Game 3, they flexed those muscles, blasting three home runs that accounted for each of their six runs.
Michael Harris II got things started in the bottom of the first, when he stepped to the plate with one out after back-to-back walks to Ronald Acuña Jr. and Matt Olson. He hammered a 2–0 sinker from Aaron Nola just over the right field wall to give Atlanta a 3–0 lead it wouldn’t relinquish.
Ozzie Albies got into the act three innings later when he launched a 96 mph four-seamer from Zack Wheeler 419 feet into the stands in right-center to increase the lead to 5–0.
Matt Olson added another in the seventh inning when he crushed a Jonathan Bowlan changeup to center to give Atlanta a 6–1 margin.
If the Braves are going to make a deep run in the playoffs, they’ll need to keep thumping baseballs out of the park. It’s the way they have played all year and it's how they were able to close out the Phillies.
The Ray Kerr Game
When the Braves announced their Game 3 starter, the collective response from the baseball world was: “Who?” We all know his name now.
Kerr had a remarkable path to signing with the Mariners as an undrafted free agent in 2017, at different points working at a movie theater and a 7-Eleven after dropping out of junior college. He bounced around the minors for several years and finally made his big league debut for the Padres at 27 years old in ’22, then recorded a 5.06 ERA in 29 games (32 innings) out of the bullpen over two seasons. He was then traded to Atlanta and recorded a 5.64 ERA in 10 games for Atlanta in 2024, but didn’t get back to the majors until Aug. 17 of this year. Once he did, he shined.
In nine appearances, he was 1–0 with a 1.47 ERA and a 0.60 WHIP. Still, he had three career starts entering Thursday night, and his team had never won any of them. The 32-year-old lefty made Atlanta manager Walt Weiss look like a genius Thursday night.
In his postseason debut, Kerr was locked in on the mound as he carved through a Phillies lineup loaded with All-Stars. He pitched 3 ⅓ shutout innings, allowing one hit, one walk and striking out two. Kerr left the game with a 3–0 lead. Atlanta’s rotation is banged up right now and they needed a big performance from whoever started Game 3. They got it from the last guy anyone expected.
Schwarber, Harper Get No Help
Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper brought the Phillies back from the dead in Game 2, hammering back-to-back home runs in the eighth inning to tie a game Philadelphia ultimately won in 10 innings. On Thursday night in Game 3, the duo combined to go 3-for-7 with a walk and a run scored. The rest of the lineup went 3-for-24 with two walks and a run. That wasn’t going to get it done.
As a team, the Phillies slashed .231/.270/.394 with 23 strikeouts over the three games, while Trea Turner went 1-for-11, Bryson Stott was 2-for-13 and J.T. Realmuto was 2-for-10. Alec Bohm was the only other hitter who showed up, going 4-for-12 with a home run. The offense that ranked 28th in wRC+ (92) during the regular season didn’t give enough support to its two main contributors, as the flaws that dogged the Phillies all year were predictably their undoing as they exited the postseason with a whimper.
If Philadelphia is going to keep its title window open, Schwarber and Harper need some help.

Bryce Harper Talks Future After Playoff Elimination, Phillies 'Will Look a Lot Different' in 2027
The Philadelphia Phillies' season ended in the American League Wild Card round on Thursday after a 6-2 loss to the Atlanta Braves.
The Phillies have plenty of questions heading into the offseason, and Bryce Harper expects the team to "look a lot different" in 2027.
"Each year's so different than the year before. I don't really put stock into years before or what happened or anything else," Harper said. "This was a brand new team. Obviously, we had the guys that are part of that core group that we are. I'd imagine this team is going to look a lot different next year with the guys that are leaving this clubhouse. So, we'll see."
Harper is tied to the Phillies through the 2031 season, so he'll remain in Philadelphia for years to come, barring a trade. Stars like Zack Wheeler, Kyle Schwarber, Trea Turner and Aaron Nola are also set to return.
But the Phillies have a handful of notable free agents, such as Alec Bohm, Jose Alvarado, Luis Arreaz, Emundo Sosa and more.
Perhaps the biggest question mark is who will be the Phillies' skipper in 2027.
Philadelphia fired manager Rob Thomson in April after a rough start to the season, and interim manager Don Mattingly helped the Phillies get back on track to reach the postseason, but he has yet to shed the interim tag.
Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic reported this week that Mattingly was "likely to be replaced" if the Phillies didn't make a deep run in the postseason, so it seems Philadelphia will be on the hunt for a new manager.
Schwarber spoke highly of Mattingly after the season ended on Thursday.
"Even when things got hard, the way that he was able to keep things at even-keel pace for us. I think that was huge," Schwarber said.
The Phillies were interested in Alex Cora after he was fired by the Boston Red Sox, but he turned the offer down. Cora said in April that he's interested in getting back into baseball at some point, but didn't clarify how soon that would be.
Even with an offseason full of changes coming, the Phillies will retain most of their core as they try to get back to the World Series. How different the team will look in the spring remains to be seen.

ATLANTA — The question of the cause of the Phillies year-over-year offensive decline had barely been finished being asked before Trea Turner had an answer.
“Me,” he said without hesitation. “I mean, it’s pretty simple. When you hit first or second, you get a lot of at-bats, and I kinda get things going. So a lot of that is on me. I think Kyle and Bryce did a good job, I scored a lot of runs, and that’s mostly because those two guys had good years. I think it starts with me and I take a lot of responsibility for that.”
Just about any way you slice it, it was a disastrous year for Turner. The season came to an end Thursday as the Phillies were eliminated by the Atlanta Braves in the NLWCS.
A year after winning the NL batting title by hitting .304, Turner finished the 2026 season with a lower on-base percentage (.297) than his batting average from the prior campaign. He did homer 19 times, but after posting a .798 OPS across his first three seasons with the Phillies, Turner finished 2026 with a .675 OPS.
Defensively, he had a major bounce back in 2025, posting two defensive runs saved, 16 outs above average and making just eight errors across 1,216 1/3 innings. In 2026, he made 21 errors, while finishing the season with minus-17 defensive runs saved and minus-eight outs above average.
President of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski did once trade Prince Fielder — just two seasons into a nine-year/$214 million contract — to the Texas Rangers for Ian Kinsler. Even though the Tigers had to send $30 million to Texas, it was one of the finest trades of Dombrowski’s career, as he offloaded a bad contract and acquired a tremendous player in the process. Perhaps Dombrowski could facilitate a similar deal this offseason, even if the Phillies don’t get nearly as much back for Turner, who is still owed more than $189 million over the next seven seasons. Of course, Turner would have to sign off on moving, as his deal includes a full no-trade clause.
Assuming Turner is back, the Phillies will have to decide whether they believe he can continue to play shortstop or not. If they believe the answer is no, the Phillies will have to A) decide what position on the field they want to move Turner to and B) sell him on the plan. Even if they can compel him to change positions, they will want him to be bought in on his new position, be it second base, left field or somewhere else.
The bigger issue wherever Turner plays defensively and hits in the lineup might be getting him back on track mentally. He’s a smart guy, one who likes to dig deep into things to try to get out of a slump. While admirable, perhaps that’s to his detriment. Turner will play next season at 34 years old, so he may not quite be at his peak athleticism anymore. But he’s still really capable in that department. The bigger issue this year, particularly in the field, seemed to be his ability to actually make the play when he put himself in position to do so. Figuring out how to help a guy mentally might be harder than teaching him a new position defensively.
Turner has been open this season about his underperformance in 2026. So what will he do this offseason to try to reset?
“That’s a good question,” Turner acknowledged. “I’ve got a lot of work to do. Kinda just go over everything and just figure out as much as I can, find answers, see what I did badly. But I feel like this year is the biggest question mark for me offensively in a long time. I gotta figure that out. I’m definitely gonna have a lot of work to do there, and I’ll do it.”

item.content:encoded:
The Braves' ace had an important matter to address before Game 3 of the National League Wild Card Series on Thursday night at Truist Park.
"First of all, I was not going to go to Chris Sale and ask him if he could pitch tonight," Weiss said after the Braves’ series-clinching 6-2 win. "I didn't want to put him in that position, because I knew that, even if he was hanging, he would tell me yes. So I was not going to bring it up."
Turns out, Weiss didn't need to.
"Literally as soon as I stepped in my office this afternoon, he was sitting in the chair across from my desk," Weiss said. "And he looked at me and he said, 'I feel amazing.'”
Weiss’ response?
“Well, let's talk."
From there, the two laid out a plan that ultimately saw Sale take down the final four outs of the Braves' first postseason series win since the 2021 World Series. Keep in mind, Sale also recorded the club's first 19 outs of this Wild Card Series as the Game 1 starter in Atlanta's 5-3 victory two days earlier.
In doing so, Sale became the first pitcher to start Game 1 of a postseason series and finish off that same series since ... Chris Sale. He previously did the same thing for the Red Sox in the 2018 World Series against the Dodgers.
Sale joined Clayton Kershaw as the only pitchers to accomplish the feat multiple times in postseason history.
"What a warrior, man," Weiss said. "This guy -- I've run out of superlatives for Chris Sale. Been talking about him all year. He's one of the best I've ever been around."
Even with Sale’s mid-afternoon ambush opening up some options for Weiss, their meticulously crafted plan only worked if all of the pieces fell into place.
Ray Kerr had to go out and do his job as the opener. Grant Holmes had to take it from there and relay the torch to a trio of relievers -- Robert Suarez, Didier Fuentes and Dylan Dodd -- who each had to take care of business.
And even then, the offense also needed to do its part. Michael Harris II checked that box early with a three-run homer in the first inning, then Ozzie Albies (a two-run shot in the fourth) and Matt Olson (a solo blast in the seventh) tacked on.
"Unbelievable. I'm just thankful for the opportunity, honestly," Sale said. "This could not be more of a group effort. This was basically a culmination of our entire year. All hands on deck. Everyone is doing everything they can to just get a win for this team."
Safe to say everything went to plan?
Well, sort of.
Knowing the plan was to pitch against the top of the Phillies' order in either the eighth or the ninth inning, Sale started to throw in the bullpen in the top of the seventh. But when Olson's homer extended the Braves' lead to 6-1 in the bottom of the seventh, it altered the strategy.
Even with Philadelphia's 9-1-2 hitters due up, Weiss instead went with the left-handed Dodd to start the eighth. He gave up a leadoff triple to pinch-hitter Derek Hill, who then scored on Trea Turner's sacrifice fly to cut the lead to four.
Needing to face at least three batters, Dodd had to stay in to face Kyle Schwarber -- the same guy who homered in the eighth inning off Dylan Lee one day earlier to trigger the Phillies' Game 2 comeback. Dodd was up to the task, though, getting MLB's regular-season home run leader to fly out for the second out.
Then, it was showtime: Sale vs. Bryce Harper.
"Electric," Harris said of the moment Sale emerged from the bullpen.
"The best," Albies said. "The minute I saw him getting warmed up, I said, 'He's definitely coming in. I love this.' The energy, the excitement there -- everybody was pumped that he came in the game."
Well, everyone except the Phillies.
Sale struck out Harper on four pitches, getting him to chase three sliders well out of the zone. The last one missed badly enough to go to the backstop, but catcher Drake Baldwin tracked it down to throw out Harper.
Now came another decision for Weiss: Let Sale go back out for the ninth or turn it over to closer Raisel Iglesias with a four-run lead?
With Iglesias warming just in case, the home crowd roared as Sale emerged from the dugout to trot back out for the ninth. Four batters later, the Braves had punched their ticket for an NLDS showdown with the Dodgers.
"Was hoping he only had to go one," Weiss said, "but he had to get to four outs."
All told, Sale -- the Braves' presumed starter for Sunday's Game 2 -- threw 21 pitches over 1 1/3 innings.
Is he still good to go for Sunday?
"I don't know. I have no idea," Weiss said. "We weren't even worried about that. It was just, 'Put this thing down and then we'll have those conversations later.' But yeah, we haven't even talked about that. It was all about tonight."
If Weiss has any doubts, he’ll certainly be getting another visit this weekend at Dodger Stadium.
"If I had to pitch tomorrow," Sale said, "I'd pitch tomorrow."

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA – While the Phillies tried to extend their season Thursday night against the Atlanta Braves at Truist Park, their Delta 757 charter sat 23 miles away at Hartsfield-Jackson International airport.
A win would send the Phillies west, to Los Angeles and a second straight National League Division Series matchup with the Dodgers.
A loss would send them home, to Philadelphia and another long, cold winter.
It didn’t take long to figure out which way the Phillies would be heading. Aaron Nola was tagged for three runs in the first inning. The Phillies never recovered. Their season came to an end in a 6-2 loss to the Braves in Game 3 of the NL Wild Card Series.
For just the second time in franchise history, the Phillies qualified for the postseason for a fifth straight year, matching a team-high streak first reached from 2007 to 2011. The Phils won the World Series in 2008, but have not since. They made a surprising run to the World Series in 2022 but were beaten by the Houston Astros in six games. They were a win away from returning to the World Series in 2023 only to collapse and lose Games 6 and 7 of the NL Championship Series at home to Arizona. Since then, they have gone the wrong way, losing in the Division Series (their first round of play) in 2024 and 2025 and now in the Wild Card Series.
“It’s always frustrating,” Kyle Schwarber said in the quiet of the losing clubhouse. “From every postseason I’ve been in, it always hurts when you’re not the last team standing.
“It’s just as frustrating this year as it was last year and the year before that.”
Philadelphia Phillies
Complete coverage of the Fightin' Phils and their MLB rivals from NBC Sports Philadelphia.
As the October defeats have mounted, the team’s core group of high-priced veteran players has gotten older.
Schwarber, always the optimist, insisted that the team’s championship window is still wide open. So did J.T. Realmuto, saying, “There’s definitely the talent in this room to win. If you watched us play all year, no matter who we played, we weren’t outmatched. It’s about execution. It’s not about the age and the years. We know we still have the talent to win.”
Over on the other side of the clubhouse, Bryce Harper didn’t sound so sure.
He was asked what gives him faith that the team can still get to where it wants to go.
“Yeah, I don’t know,” he said. “It’s going to be a long offseason, obviously. I have trust in the organization and the people that are in charge. We’ll see where we go.”
Heading into the offseason, the Phils have many questions, first and foremost: Will Don Mattingly return as manager in 2027? He took over, with an interim tag, for Rob Thomson after the team got off to a 9-19 start in April.
The Phillies played .590 ball (79-55) under Mattingly, but president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski tried to hire Alex Cora when he let Thomson go, and he seems likely to try again in the coming weeks. Stay tuned.
Mattingly would not touch the topic after the game. Schwarber, Realmuto, Nola and Trea Turner all said they’d like to see Mattingly return. Harper declined to talk about the topic.
If Cora comes on board, he will be taking over a team of highs and lows, one with an inconsistent offense that is seemingly up one month (see August) and down the next (see September). He will be taking over a team that lacks pitching depth, both in the starting rotation and the bullpen. Both weaknesses reared their head in recent weeks as the Phils had to scramble to make the playoffs, using ace Zack Wheeler on the final day of the regular season, a circumstance that prevented him from starting Game 1 of the postseason.
Wheeler mentioned the team’s overall inconsistency when asked if he believed the Phils still had the talent to make a deeper postseason run next year.
“Consistency in every group, I think that’s what will get us there,” he said. “We were kind of inconsistent throughout the year. Maybe we were hitting, but we weren’t pitching well. Maybe we were pitching well and we weren’t hitting well. We just have to put it all together throughout the majority of the season.
“We’re hungry, that’s for sure. We just didn’t get the job done.”
The Phils had chances to win the series.
Jesus Luzardo pitched well in Game 1 and they held a 3-2 lead in the seventh. With few trusted arms in his leaky bullpen, Mattingly went to his All-Star closer, Jhoan Duran, in the bottom of the seventh. Duran got through that inning but gave up the lead on a three-run homer in the eighth and the Phillies lost, 5-3.
They bounced back to win a wild Game 2 Wednesday in 10 innings on the strength of three late home runs and the clutch pitching of Cristopher Sanchez, Alex McFarlane and Andrew Painter. They seemed to have momentum heading into Game 3.
But the momentum disappeared quickly as Nola had big trouble throwing strikes.
Just three of the right-hander's first 13 pitches to open the game were strikes. He fell behind Ronald Acuna Jr., and Matt Olson, the Braves’ Nos. 2 and 3 hitters, with 3-0 counts and eventually walked both. He then fell behind Michael Harris II, 2-0. Harris hit the next pitch, a sinker down and out of the zone, over the right-field wall for a three-run homer.
“I think he was just a little too careful,” Realmuto said of Nola. “I don’t think he was way off because he was just missing. They just did a good job of not chasing and making him come in the zone. When a lineup is good like that and they get on a roll, it’s tough to get them out when they’re not chasing.”
Nola did not make it through the second inning. Tim Mayza got the final out of the frame before handing off to Wheeler in the top of the third. The Phillies’ brain trust opted not to start Wheeler on three days’ rest. He'd never done that before. Also, Wheeler admitted that at this point of the season, he wasn’t feeling 100 percent. It was decided that Nola’s best chance of succeeding would be to stay in a starter’s role.
“We’re going to need Nola in this game,” Mattingly said before the game. “Starting him gives us the best version of him.”
The Phillies weren’t sure Wheeler would even be able to pitch until he tested himself by playing catch before the game. He ended up pitching four innings but was not particularly sharp. He gave up three hits and walked three. One of those walks turned into a run when Ozzie Albies stroked a two-run homer in the fourth to give the Braves a 5-0 lead.
“We felt Nola was on solid rest,” Mattingly said after the game. “If he could get us into the game at all, we’d have Zack after that. Obviously, it didn’t go well.”
Atlanta used lefty Ray Kerr as an opener. He pitched 3 1/3 innings and did not allow a run. The only hit Kerr gave up was a single to Schwarber in the first inning. Kerr then struck out Harper.
Grant Holmes, Robert Suarez, Didier Fuentes, Dylan Dodd and Chris Sale finished off the Phillies. Sale, the Braves’ ace lefty who started Game 1, entered with two outs in the eighth and struck out Harper.
Before the 2019 season, Harper signed a 13-year, $330-million contract with the Phillies. He came looking for a parade down Broad Street. Eight years later, he boarded a flight back to Philadelphia, still looking.

ATLANTA -- Ray Kerr was the left-handed reliever the Braves chose to get through Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper during the first inning of Game 3 of the National League Wild Card Series against the Phillies.
Kerr served as the opener in Thursday's series-clinching 6-2 win and dazzled, keeping the Phillies in check with 3 1/3 scoreless innings, allowing one hit and one walk with two strikeouts. Grant Holmes followed Kerr and allowed one run on two hits and one walk, while earning the win.
“This was just another Thursday,” Kerr said. “Growing up, I had a hard time. So, this was nothing.”
The Braves provided a clue they would go this way in Miami on Friday, when they used Kerr as an opener on Holmes’ scheduled start date.
“That was a best-case scenario, and [Kerr] did it,” Weiss said. “He got through the top twice, which kept us from using another guy at the top. So, Ray -- it all started with Ray. Everything fell into place because of Ray Kerr.”
Kerr posted a 1.47 ERA over 18 1/3 innings in nine appearances going back to his Aug. 17 season debut. Left-handed hitters were 4-for-23 (.174) against him in the regular season, with one extra-base hit, a double.
Kerr made two appearances against the Phillies in September, with the most recent a three-inning outing on Sept. 13. He got Schwarber to ground into a double play and then struck out Trea Turner to end the fifth. Harper began the sixth with a double but was left stranded.
Kerr has made just 19 big league appearances since the start of 2024. After tossing three scoreless innings against the Marlins on Friday, he said he would gladly welcome the chance to be an opener in the postseason.
Holmes posted a 3.57 ERA in 29 starts this season and a 2.94 ERA over his final 14 starts. Opponents produced a .590 OPS against him the first time facing him in a game and an .886 OPS during the second plate appearance.

item.content:encoded:
What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa.
The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the postseason on Wednesday so let’s jump straight into the action!
AL Wild Card Series Game 2
Chicago White Sox 7, Houston Astros 3
(Chicago wins 2-0)
After just two games, I can’t think of any playoff participant who wants to face these White Sox. That is a sentence that no one could conceive of typing at the start of the season. Two seasons removed from suffering the most losses in MLB history and on the back of three straight losing campaigns, this upstart Chicago squad came out of nowhere to crash the postseason, starting with a two game sweep of the Astros in their own building.
They have done so by scoring early and often, the White Sox lineup a deep unit one-thru-nine with multiple ways to hurt you. They work deep counts, foul pitches off, draw walks, and can put the ball in play, but can also slug the ball out of the yard from almost any spot in the batting order. On Tuesday, they scored three unanswered runs in the first two innings to put the Astros on the back foot from the word go, and Wednesday continued the trend with the Southsiders hanging a four-spot before the home team had a chance to bat.
They had a 1-0 lead just five pitches into the game against Astros ace Hunter Brown, Sam Antonacci leading off with a double before Kyle Teel drove him home with a single. A fielding error by Nick Allen on a Miguel Vargas grounder put a pair on, and three straight singles by Andrew Benintendi, Tristan Peters, and Chase Meidroth plated three more runs with help from a Lucas Spence throwing error from center.
Credit to the Astros, they did not roll over after going down four in the first and slowly chipped into the White Sox lead. Jeremy Peña led off the bottom of the first with a booming home run that clattered off the left field wall just below the train tracks. Cam Smith hit one to almost exactly the same spot with two outs in the second. Jose Altuve narrowly snuck a solo shot into the Crawford Boxes to lead off the fourth and just like that, a 4-0 game had become a 4-3 thriller.
An inning later it looked like the Astros would pull of the improbable and complete the comeback. Smith was hit by a pitch, Peña singled, and Isaac Paredes walked to load the bases with two outs for Altuve. However, reliever Anthony Kay got Altuve to fly out to medium right field to strand all three ducks on the pond. That left the door open for the White Sox to swing the momentum back in their own favor and they did so immediately. Benintendi and Peters drew a pair of walks to open the sixth, prompting Joe Espada to call on Bryan Abreu out of the bullpen. Astros owner Jim Crane vetoed a trade of Abreu to the Twins in the final minutes of the deadline, and Abreu rewarded that faith by hanging a 3-1 slider to Meidroth, the second baseman crushing a three-run bomb to left to put the final nail in the Astros’ coffin.
After sweeping this rematch of the 2005 World Series, the White Sox advance to the ALDS where they will face the AL Central champion Guardians, first pitch of Game 1 scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET on Saturday.
NL Wild Card Series Game 2
Philadelphia Phillies 4, Atlanta Braves 3
(Series tied 1-1)
The Phillies’ season was hanging by a thread until some late heroics by Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper, and Alec Bohm sent this thrilling series to a decisive Game 3. It was a pitchers’ duel early between two starters trending in opposite directions. Tyler Mahle entered his first career playoff start with a sub-two ERA after joining the Braves from the Giants at the deadline while Cristopher Sánchez posted an ERA above five in the month of September (though will still likely wrap up his second straight runner-up finish in NL Cy Young balloting).
The one thing the two starters do have in common is first inning struggles and that certainly played out in this game. Mahle allowed a leadoff double to Trea Turner and consecutive one-out singles by Bryce Harper and Alex Bohm to allow the Phillies to jump ahead, 1-0. However, Sánchez issued a leadoff walk to Ronald Acuña Jr., who promptly stole second and scored the tying run on a Matt Olson single.
Both starters settled in from there, trading zeroes for the next five innings, until things unraveled for Sánchez and his defense in the seventh. Sean Murphy worked a leadoff walk and Ha-Seong Kim reached on a bunt single to put a pair on with no outs. Drake Baldwin then clubbed what looked like a routine liner to right, but Harper misplayed it horrifically breaking in on the ball only to watch it sail over his glove and to the wall for what was ruled as an RBI double. Sánchez intentionally walked Ozzie Albies to load the bases, and Olson made him pay with a sac fly to double the Braves lead, 3-1.
What should have been a hammer blow to the Phillies morale did not play out as such. Schwarber immediately responded with a towering leadoff shot off lefty reliever Dylan Lee, and Harper atoned for his misplay by going back-to-back to retie the game, 3-3. That sent this game to extra innings, where the much-maligned Alec Bohm continued his redemption tour. Bohm was on the bubble of being non-tendered during the offseason, but the Phillies kept him around and drove in the first run of the series with an RBI double in the first inning of Game 1. The third baseman was the ultimate hero in this one, his opposite field solo homer off rookie Didier Fuentes in the 10th to keep the Phillies season alive and force a decisive Game 3.
San Diego Padres 4, Chicago Cubs 1
(San Diego wins 2-0)
This game featured surprisingly quick hooks of both starters as neither manager wanted to risk leaving their highest leverage relievers unused. One was certainly more deserved than the other, Kevin Gausman allowing three runs on five hits in 3.1 innings. The Cubs were desperate for starting pitching at the Trade Deadline and Gausman was supposed to be their big prize. However, he flopped after making the move from the Blue Jays, pitching to a 4.83 ERA in nine starts post-deadline, and his stinker tonight was the beginning of the end of the Cubs’ season. Nick Pivetta on the other hand held Chicago to a run on three hits and two walks with four strikeouts in 3.1 innings, but Craig Stammen seemed determined to play the matchups in this one.
Ty France got things started with a double to lead off the second, advancing to third on a Jackson Merrill single, who then stole second to put a pair in scoring position for Xander Bogaerts. The veteran shortstop opened the scoring with an RBI single, which brought Ethan Salas to the plate. The 20-year-old became the youngest catcher ever to appear in a playoff game, and in his first postseason PA, he lifted a sac fly to center to plate Merrill as the Padres’ second run.
The real story of this series has been the Cubs’ inability to score. They led MLB scoring 5.25 runs per game, spearheaded by shoo-in NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong and his MLB-leading 45 home runs (PCA would go 0-for-7 with four strikeouts in the series). They found themselves shut out through the first 12.1 innings of this series, finally breaking the seal in the fourth on a Seiya Suzuki single, Ian Happ walk, and Nico Hoerner RBI single. A Carson Kelly hit-by-pitch loaded the bases with two outs, but Dansby Swanson flew out to stand all three in place.
San Diego immediately punished them for failing to fully cash in on that scoring opportunity. Bogaerts reached on a one-out double, prompting Craig Counsell to call on Daniel Palencia in relief of Gausman. Palencia yanked a 101 mph fastball right into Sheets’ nitro zone down and in, and the lefty crushed it to right for a mammoth two-run blast.
It was all hands on deck from there from the Padres bullpen looking to protect their lead for the final five innings of the contest. They proved how terrifying a relief corps they’ve been all season, allowing just three base runners — a Michael Busch walk with two outs in the fifth, a Tyrone Taylor pinch-hit single with one out in the eighth, and a Hoerner one-out double off Mason Miller in the ninth — after the Cubs stranded the bases loaded to end the fourth.
San Diego advances to the NLDS where they will face the best team in baseball. It’s an unenviable position to come up against presumptive NL Cy Young Jacob Misiorowski and the 103-win Brewers. Game 1 of that series is scheduled for October 3rd with first pitch time contingent upon the result of Game 3 between Philly and Atlanta.

October 01, 2026
It feels sort of unexpected, that the Phillies are not only alive, but have some momentum with the third and final game of the NL Wild Card Series in Atlanta set for Thursday night.
Just one win, and the Phillies can hop on a flight to Los Angeles to try and get revenge against the Dodgers for last season's NLDS failure.
Before Game 3's first pitch, we have a few Phillies' thoughts we'd like to share:
How are we feeling about Aaron Nola — named Game 3's starter earlier Thursday morning? In his 15 starts prior to last Saturday's bizarre three run first inning and out for the Phillies' veteran, Nola boasted a pretty solid 3.12 ERA which is more in line with the Nola who got a monster free agent contract a few offseasons ago.
He's also got some postseason pedigree. He's started 11 playoff games over the last five Octobers, and his two worst starts actually came during the World Series run in 2022. In six starts since 2023, he has a 3.00 ERA and 3-2 record. Is he better than Zack Wheeler pitching on three days rest for the first time ever? The Phils coaching staff made their choice and it's a reasonable one, if nothing else.
If Alec Bohm is parting ways with the Phillies in a few weeks — his contract is set to expire and the Phillies are likely to let him walk and give top prospect Aidan Miller the chance to start the season at third (or second) in 2027 — he gave Phillies fans a spectacular parting gift.
ALEC BOHM GO-AHEAD HOMER
PHILLIES LEAD IN THE 10TH 🤯 pic.twitter.com/S4wFOFyDq1
By virtue of all three other Wild Card series' wrapping up (more on that in a second), the Phillies have Thursday all to themselves and have moved from a 2 p.m. start to prime time (at 8:15 on NBC).
The Phillies are no strangers to primetime playoff starts — they've had a ton of them over the last half decade. They also play better at night. Their win percentage under the lights (55.5%, 61-49) is better than during the afternoon (51%, 26-25). With some extra time for their pitchers to rest and prepare, this is probably a net positive move for the Phillies.
As we just mentioned, the other three series' ended with a 2-0 sweep. Since the league switched to the three-game Wild Card first round format, teams who win Game 1 are now 24-3. The Phillies have a chance to be the fourth.
Philadelphia also has the chance to be the first team in franchise history to win a playoff series (albeit a short one) after losing a Game 1. They are 0-9 historically when they start a series off with a loss.
Another mark, probably, in the Phillies' advantage column is that they're going up against a Braves team unprepared to send a third starter out there. Lefty reliever Ray Kerr — with an impressive 1.77 ERA this season — is going to start the game, likely to face the lefty-heavy front of the Phillies order (Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber). Perhaps the Phillies should consider splitting these hitters up and having Schwarber bat lead off, with Trea Turner second and Harper third?
After Kerr, it's expected the Braves will go to righty starter Grant Holmes, who has a 3.44 ERA this season. Holmes faced the Phillies four times during the regular season and the Phils' hitters will all have recent recollections of facing him.
The Phillies will see how far they can get behind Nola, but it'll be interesting to see who's the next man in. Will it be Jesús Luzardo who pitched in Game 1? Will they ultimately call on Wheeler (or optimistically save him for an NLDS Game 1)? Can Andrew Painter throw on back-to-back days?

item.content:encoded:
He removed his cap and sat in a crouch with two outs in the seventh inning on Wednesday afternoon at Truist Park. Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly had just walked to the mound to remove Cristopher Sánchez from the game, two batters after Harper’s misplay on a fly ball to right sparked Atlanta’s go-ahead two-run rally in Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series. Guns N’ Roses blasted throughout the ballpark as the Braves reveled in Harper’s misfortune.
“Obviously a world of emotion there,” Harper said. “I'll tell you what. I was thinking about Krew, my son, what I would say to him in that situation.”
The Phillies were six outs from another crushing season-ending loss and perhaps significant offseason changes. But then the unbelievable happened. The Phillies won in 10 innings, 4-3. Kyle Schwarber and Harper hit back-to-back homers in the eighth inning to tie it. Alec Bohm hit an opposite-field homer in the 10th to take the lead. Rookie Andrew Painter pitched three scoreless innings of relief in the first postseason performance of his career.
“What a sport,” Harper said.
“A great gift,” said Jesús Luzardo, celebrating his 29th birthday.
“It’s in our DNA,” Schwarber said. “We’re just not going to quit.”
Thursday's Game 3, airing on NBC and Peacock, will start at 8 p.m. ET.
Sánchez allowed a leadoff walk in the seventh inning to Sean Murphy. Ha-Seong Kim bunted a ball toward the mound. Bohm, who turned a fantastic 3-2-3 double play to end the sixth, inexplicably tried to get the lead runner at second base. He did not.
Two batters later, Harper misjudged Drake Baldwin’s fly ball to right. It tipped over the top of his glove to allow a run to score.
Sánchez found Harper in the dugout afterward.
“I told him that he was bound to have a great moment,” Sánchez said via team interpreter Diego D’Aniello.
“I just tapped him on the butt and said, ‘You’ve got this,’” J.T. Realmuto said.
Schwarber started the inning against Braves left-hander Dylan Lee, who hadn’t allowed a homer to a left-hander in 92 at-bats this season. He hit a 3-2 slider a Statcast-projected 447 feet. Braves right fielder Ronald Acuña Jr. didn’t even bother to turn around to watch the ball leave the ballpark.
Harper greeted Schwarber at home plate.
“Hey, man, just try to find a way on,” Schwarber told Harper.
Instead, Harper smashed a 1-1 slider to right field to tie the game.
“I wasn't not trying to hit a homer, I can tell you that,” Harper said. “For me, everybody is going to make mistakes at some point, but it's how you come through in the next situation.
“It's not that serious, to tell you the truth. I think people take it very seriously -- and don't get me wrong, I take it serious. But I think there's a mindset, especially for kids nowadays, is parents and coaches put so much on kids these days to have to come through and be great. But for me, it's, 'How can you learn from each situation that you're in to come out great in the next one?'”
It was one of the more dramatic moments in Phillies postseason history considering how everything had unfolded in the bottom of the seventh inning, with the Phillies’ season and future of the organization on the line.
“What just happened,” reliever Tim Mayza said.
“That wasn’t stressful at all,” Zack Wheeler said.
Painter put up zeros to give the Phillies a chance to win it in the 10th.
“That’s a career-altering performance in my opinion,” Realmuto said.
Bohm hit the go-ahead homer in the 10th against Didier Fuentes.
“I didn't know it was gone until I heard it hit -- kind of rattle against the fence above the wall,” Bohm said.
It was Bohm’s first opposite-field home run since Opening Day. Bohm became the fourth player in Phillies history to hit a go-ahead homer in extra innings of a postseason game, joining George Vukovich (1981 NLDS Game 4), Lenny Dykstra (1993 NLDS Game 5) and Realmuto (2022 World Series Game 1).
“I've seen some great ones that this has happened to,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “I saw one of the greatest. I was at shortstop when Kirk Gibson did his thing off one of the greatest closers [Dennis Eckersley] of all time [in Game 1 of the 1988 World Series]. It comes with the territory when you're pitching late in close games. Every once in a while, they get you.”
But it’s not over yet. The Phillies need to win Thursday to keep their season alive. They are 1-3 in franchise history in win-or-go-home postseason games. They won Game 5 of the 1980 NLCS. They lost Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS, Game 5 of the 2011 NLDS and Game 5 of the 1981 NLDS.
“We have to keep going,” Schwarber said.
Painter struck out Dominic Smith looking on an 0-2 fastball -- after an appropriately dramatic and successful challenge by Realmuto, the first game-ending ABS challenge in postseason history -- to end the game at 5:19 p.m. ET. Trea Turner, who went 1-for-5 with a double, returned to the Phillies’ clubhouse by himself 32 minutes later.
He had just left the batting cage near the visitors’ dugout. He carried two bats in each hand.
He had been working, preparing for Game 3.
“Never a doubt,” Turner said about the win.

The Atlanta Braves are one win away from a trip to the National League Division Series and a date with the back-to-back World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers. They fell into an early 1-0 hole against the Philadelphia Phillies in Game 2 of the NL wild card series, but that didn't stop star outfielder Ronald Acuna Jr. from doing something special that has only been done twice in Braves history.
With the Braves down 1-0, Acuna stole two bases in the bottom of the first inning and ultimately scoring the team's first run on Matt Olson's RBI single to tie the game up. According to Sarah Langs of MLB.com, Acuna has joined two Braves legends on an all-exclusive list.
Ronald Acuna Jr. makes Braves history
Acuna has also become the seventh player in postseason history with two stolen bases in the first inning of a game. That was last done by Phillies star shortstop Trea Turner in Game 2 of the NL Division Series against the New York Mets.
But it still has been a very long time since a member of the Braves accomplished this feat. Rafael Furcal was last with the Braves in 2005, so it has been over two decades since a Braves player has pulled this off.
Acuna is a former MVP, NL Rookie of the Year, three-time Silver Slugger and five-time All-Star. He is signed through this season and has club options for 2027 and 2028.
During the regular season, the 28-year-old outfielder hit .255/.345/.451 with 20 home runs, 55 RBI, 21 stolen bases and a .796 OPS. Injuries limited him to 107 games, but he has started the postseason off with a bang and is a big reason why the Braves are now pointed towards the NLDS.
But along with his power and solid defense has come some elite speed and baserunning, and he put that on full display in Game 2 as the Braves punched back from an early deficit against the Phillies and put themselves in position to potentially advance to the next round.
The postseason is always full of historic moments, and Acuna created one of his own with his speed on the basepaths. It will be interesting to see if the Braves can ultimately take Game 2 and effectively end the Phillies' season. A win advances them to the next round.

The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series.
The Diamondbacks, despite their late push, fell short of the playoffs, thanks to a Phillies win on Sunday against the Rays. Meanwhile, the final domino to fall in the American League went in favor of the Astros, who secured the AL West title with a victory over the Athletics on Sunday. Houston becomes the worst team to ever make the playoffs in a 162-game season, sneaking in and winning the division with just an 81–81 record.
Fans won’t have to wait long for postseason to get underway, with the Wild Card series set to begin on Tuesday. But before the action gets going, we’re going to do a final power ranking, assessing where all 12 teams sit and detailing their biggest strength and weakness.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching, lineup
Biggest weakness: Bullpen
The Dodgers may be the No. 2 seed in the National League, but they’re built to win in October. It’s hard to determine what’s a greater strength between their loaded starting rotation or their star-studded lineup. There’s no weaknesses in their rotation, with All-Star caliber pitchers available to take the mound every night, even with Shohei Ohtani restricted to DH duties. There isn’t a team in MLB with more postseason experience than Los Angeles, who have won back-to-back World Series with this core. During the regular season, the Dodgers had MLB’s second-highest OPS (.762) and fourth-best ERA (3.55). If there’s any way to beat them it’s by getting after a bullpen that has been inconsistent throughout the season, though it’s still a top-10 unit. Injuries have plagued their relief pitching corps, however, with the likes of Blake Treinen, Edgardo Henriquez and Will Klein all currently on IL.
2. Milwaukee Brewers
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Brewers’ rotation, headlined by NL Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski, has been one of MLB’s best, and it’s helped the team secure the league’s best regular-season record. The starting rotation owns MLB’s fifth-best ERA (3.65) and their bullpen has been equally impressive, ranking third in MLB with a 3.40 ERA. Milwaukee has scored the second-most runs in the league this season (832), as their small-ball approach has worked wonders for them. But in October, when a single swing of the bat can dramatically change a team’s fortunes and rallies are harder to come by, they might not have the power hitters capable of providing that big home run swing. The Brewers didn’t have a single 30-home run hitter this season and had just three everyday starters with a slugging percentage above .450.
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Bottom-third of the lineup
The Rays had the best record in the American League this season, largely thanks to their pitching. The starting rotation has been excellent, ranking third in MLB with a 3.51 ERA. Drew Rasmussen has quietly been one of MLB’s best arms, and Freddy Peralta has begun to rediscover his previous form after a rough go with the Mets and a shaky start on the mound in Tampa. Much like the Brewers, the Rays primarily utilize a small-ball approach offensively. The Rays hit the ninth-fewest home runs in MLB this year, and despite rostering some elite hitters such as Junior Caminero and Yandy Diaz, they haven’t received much production out of the bottom third of their lineup, which is their biggest weakness with the postseason looming.
4. Atlanta Braves
Biggest strength: Deep lineup
Biggest weakness: Plate discipline, low on-base rates
The Braves are another team with an abundance of postseason experience in the lineup. They have several players that can turn a game on its head with one swing of the bat, and had five 20-plus home run hitters during the regular season in Matt Olson, Michael Harris, Drake Baldwin, Ozzie Albies and Ronald Acuña Jr. Although the lineup is flush with talent, the group has a tendency to chase pitches out of the zone, and they don’t draw walks at a high rate. The Braves ranked 28th in MLB in on-base percentage (.309) during the regular season, often opting for an aggressive approach at the plate rather than a patient one. That could prove costly in October against some of the best pitchers in the sport, where slowing the game down and getting runners on base by any means necessary will be crucial.
5. New York Yankees
Biggest strength: Elite pitching rotation
Biggest weakness: Offense (without Aaron Judge), high strikeout rates
Yankees starting pitchers led MLB with a 3.30 ERA this season, and they’ll have one of the best rotations in the postseason with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon set to take the mound in October. The bullpen has been a bit inconsistent, but they should be able to ride their starting rotation deep into games. The biggest weakness for the Yankees is their lineup, particularly without Aaron Judge in the mix. New York had the sixth-most strikeouts this season and were tied for 11th in MLB with a .720 OPS. With Judge out of the lineup, however, their OPS falls to a .690 mark, which would be 29th in MLB.
6. San Diego Padres
Biggest strength: Elite bullpen
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Padres’ bullpen has been as reliable as they come this season, and the team flexes multiple elite relievers who they can reliably turn the ball over to in the later innings in Mason Miller, Yuki Matsui and Adrian Morejon, among others. San Diego has shaken off a slow start to the year and are playing at an extremely high level heading into the postseason. The offense is alive again after a dreadful first couple of months of the season, with players like Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill having been among MLB’s best second-half performers at the plate. The starting pitching will be the x-factor in October, however. With Casey Mize landing on the IL, their options in the rotation are even thinner. Remaining competitive within the first six innings will be crucial for the Padres, whose starting pitchers rank 21st in MLB with a 4.42 ERA this year.
7. Chicago Cubs
Biggest strength: Dominant lineup
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Cubs have had MLB’s best offense this season, leading the league in OPS (.767), walks (674), runs scored (850) and slugging percentage (.428). They’ve been particularly elite since the All-Star break, logging a .797 OPS in their last 66 games. With Pete Crow-Armstrong playing at an MVP level and Alex Bregman having enjoyed a monster second half, the Cubs’ offense will be tough to shut down in October. Of course, they’ll need their pitching to live up to their end of the bargain, which it’s struggled to do this season. Chicago’s starting pitching has been disappointing and plagued by injuries. The starting rotation ranks 18th in MLB with a 4.27 ERA this year and have surrendered the third-most home runs (142).
8. Boston Red Sox
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Inconsistent offense
The Red Sox’s pitching as a whole has been excellent. Boston’s bullpen owns a league-best 3.00 ERA this season, and no group of relievers in MLB has surrendered fewer home runs (55). Their starters have been great, too, ranking eighth in the league with a 3.92 ERA, and they boast a solid mix of veterans (Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez) and young, emerging starters (Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett). Offensively, however, the Red Sox have been prone to spells of inconsistency. They started the season ice cold before enjoying a scalding hot summer streak, but they’ve come crashing back down to earth in the final month of the season. The Red Sox rank dead last in MLB in OPS (.651) throughout the month of September, and they’re batting a league-worst .219 in that span.
9. Cleveland Guardians
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Guardians starting pitching has been a top-10 unit this season, ranking ninth in ERA (3.93) and fifth in strikeouts (878). Parker Messick has been superb in his first full season in MLB, and Gavin Williams has emerged as one of the league’s best strikeout pitchers. Cleveland will feel confident with those two spearheading the rotation, but they may struggle to get the run support required to take advantage of their quality starters. The Guardians rank 24th in MLB with 678 runs scored, 26th in OPS (.696) and 27th in home runs (162) this season. If they can’t come up with some big at-bats, it won’t matter how effective their pitching is in October.
10. Philadelphia Phillies
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Defense, bullpen
The Phillies have one of the best starting rotations in MLB, but they’ve been plagued by some underperforming position players and a lackluster bullpen. There’s arguably no better trio of starters in MLB than Cristopher Sánchez, Zack Wheeler and Jesús Luzardo. The team’s starting rotation ranks seventh in the league with a 3.80 ERA, but their bullpen ranks 21st in ERA (4.43). Defensively, the Phillies have been atrocious, too. Only the Athletics have fewer defensive runs saved than the Phillies’ -43, according to the Fielding Bible, and the infield has been a serious concern, with Trea Turner, Bryce Harper and Alec Bohm all ranking among the bottom 26 defensive players (of 270 qualified players) in MLB in terms of outs above average, per Statcast. Defensive shortcomings and mishaps could prove highly costly in October, and that’s an area that’s plagued Philadelphia all season.
11. Chicago White Sox
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The White Sox have a potent lineup and are the only team in MLB that have three players who hit 30 or more home runs in Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery. Chicago hit the fifth-most home runs this season (211) and scored the fifth-most runs (776). While the offense is among the league’s best in terms of power, the White Sox starting pitching is a serious concern. The starting rotation posted a season ERA of 4.60 (fourth-worst in MLB), a 1.34 WHIP (sixth-worst in MLB) and recorded the third-fewest strikeouts of any starting rotation in the league. Chicago’s starters also threw the fewest innings in MLB this season, often struggling to get deep into games before the baton was passed to the bullpen. If the starting rotation can’t keep runs off the board, it might not matter how explosive their lineup can be.
12. Houston Astros
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
Yordan Alvarez is likely to win the AL MVP, and he’s the type of hitter teams will not be eager to pitch to in October. No team in MLB hit more home runs than the Astros, who hit 226. In addition to Alvarez’s 42, Houston had four other players with 20-plus homers, including Christian Walker (29), Isaac Paredes (25), Jeremy Peña (22) and Cam Smith (21). They don’t have much to worry about offensively, but their lineup will need to produce in order to ease the burden on their starting rotation, which has largely struggled this year. Hunter Brown remains a reliable ace, but beyond him there’s a lack of experience and talent within the rotation. Astros starters ranked 27th in MLB with a 4.81 ERA and 1.40 WHIP, both of which were the worst among all teams that qualified for the postseason, and they walked the most batters in MLB this season. If the lineup can’t make up for the rotation’s shortcomings, it could be a short postseason stint for Houston this year.
Karl Rasmussen is a staff writer for Sports Illustrated. A University of Oregon alum who joined SI in February 2023, his work has appeared on 12up and ClutchPoints. Rasmussen is a loyal Tottenham, Jets, Yankees and Ducks fan.

item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.

Phillips also co-hosts The Assembly Call Podcast about Indiana Hoosiers basketball and previously worked at Bleacher Report. He is a proud San Diego native and a graduate of Indiana University’s journalism program.
